solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

passage_flags: minor: P1 defines local noon as when the sun 'stood highest' (apparent solar noon), but most towns actually kept local MEAN time, which can differ from sundial noon by up to ~16 minutes; P3 then speaks of zones keeping 'mean time.' Not fatal at ACT level, but slightly inconsistent.

Historical claims check out: General Time Convention (railroads' association) adopted four US zones in 1883; Sunday, Nov. 18, 1883 is correct; telegraph time signals coordinated the switch; Standard Time Act of 1918; Boston local noon precedes New York's; 1 degree per 4 minutes is correct; towns east of their meridian set clocks back ('Day of Two Noons').
minor: 'The sun did not move' is rhetorical (the sun appears to move, per P1); harmless but could confuse a literal reader.

flags: Weak distractors: A is contradicted outright by P4 ('No act of Congress required it'), D is the opposite of the passage, C (trains ran late) is never mentioned; only B is plausible, so the item is near-giveaway.
minor: B closely paraphrases the passage's final paragraph ('noon became an agreement'), making it a lookup for students who read the ending.
R037-01.notes: Passage culminates in the shift of time from a solar fact to a shared agreement, driven by railroads.

flags: minor: Some students may confuse 'sun moves westward' with west reaching noon first and pick A; that is the only real trap.
R037-02.notes: Boston (east) before New York before Chicago; a town farther west reaches noon still later.

flags: minor: B and D are implausible; C is the opposite of the situation described (before 1883).
R037-03.notes: Several clocks, each correct for some line, none for the street = confusion from each railroad keeping its own time.

flags: minor: 'at set times' is a light inference (passage says trains 'had to meet and pass at sidings'); otherwise close paraphrase, effectively a lookup. Distractors A, B, D have no support.
R037-04.notes: Opposing trains on one track had to meet at sidings; a time mismatch risks collision.

flags: minor: B is the intended reversal trap (forward vs. back); C and D are unsupported.

minor: A says clocks were 'set back to noon,' which presumes the reset happened just after local noon; the passage says clocks were 'turned back several minutes, and noon arrived a second time,' so A is a fair paraphrase.
R037-05.notes: P3: east of the central meridian, local noon had passed; clocks turned back, so noon came again.

flags: minor: 'missed why the change succeeded' is an inference from 'They had something more effective, which was a network'; reasonable but not stated. A is a well-built reversal trap (it calls the legal claim mistaken, but the author says they were 'correct').
R037-06.notes: 'They were, in a sense, correct: the railroads had no legal authority' = agreement; 'in a sense' plus the 'something more effective' point = qualified.

R037-07.notes: 'What is striking is who made the change' = notable/remarkable. Forceful is the literal-meaning trap.

flags: minor: C (two clocks disagree) is the main lure because it echoes P2, but it shows the old confusion, not noon-as-agreement. A and D show the old sun-based meaning.
R037-08.notes: Under standard time, clocks read noon by convention even when the sun is not highest (e.g., a town west of its meridian).

flags: minor: Overlaps in content with R037-06 (both turn on P4's 'no legal authority, yet adopted' point) and partly with R037-01; the choices do not give away another answer, though.
minor: B, C, D are unsupported claims that few would choose; borderline easy.
R037-09.notes: Law came 35 years after railroads adopted it; the public followed by practice ('much of the public followed').

set_notes: Answer distribution: A x3 (03, 05, 09), B x2 (01, 08), C x2 (04, 07), D x2 (02, 06). No item's choices reveal another's key. Set skews easy (6 easy, 3 medium, 0 hard); there is no genuinely hard item. Mild overlaps: 01/08 (noon as convention) and 06/09 (railroads acting without law).
